title: Claude Cowork skills: How they work and what to build
content:
If you’ve yet to understand Claude Cowork skills, let me help you out: Claude Cowork is a mode that can access your desktop files and complete tasks for you. A skill is a set of instructions that tell Claude exactly how to perform a specific workflow. When combined, the two can boost your productivity in a way that Claude Chat alone cannot.
Claude skills aren’t limited to one Claude surface or tool. Skills work in Claude Chat, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. So “Claude Cowork skills” are actually a feature across the AI, not just a single mode.
This is even truer since Anthropic announced that Claude Cowork, Chat, Artifacts, and Design are merging into a single unified experience, starting in October 2026. Skills, projects, connectors, and tasks all carry over, but users no longer have to dance between tabs. Claude simply decides which tools to use based on what you ask.
These changes are meant to reduce confusion, but it’s natural to still have questions. We’ll clear things up as they stand now, share what Claude Cowork skills are, and what you should build to get the most out of them.
Note: These changes are rolling out to Claude’s Pro and Max plans first, on the web, desktop, and mobile over the coming weeks, with plans to extend them to the free and team tiers later.
A Claude Cowork Skill is a reusable instruction folder (with optional supporting templates, scripts, or reference documents attached) that Claude loads when a task needs it, and ignores when it doesn’t. You can use Claude Cowork skills across every other Claude surface, so truly, any Claude skill is a Claude Cowork skill and vice versa.
If you want to get into the nuts and bolts of it, a Claude skill is technically a folder that can contain the following:
What makes a skill different from a detailed prompt you paste every time is:
Thanks to Cowork and the recent merger, a skill can now also access internal documentation and do things like reading and writing to folders on your computer, running multi-step tasks autonomously, coordinating sub-agents , and producing finished files like spreadsheets and presentations, not just responding in text like it would with Chat alone.
When you need Claude to repeat a multi-step process the same way every time (i.e., formatting a weekly report, triaging leads, summarizing support tickets), that’s where a skill comes in handy.
For example, when I’m using Claude for fact-checking assistance, I often prompt it with detailed instructions on what to verify in the article, how to verify it, and what to include in its citations so that I can double-check its work. Instead of repeating that prompt every single time I’m done with an article, I have a “blog-fact-checker” skill that contains my detailed instructions. Now, instead of 500 words, I simply type two words, “Fact check,” and attach my draft via Google Docs. Easy.
Note: Record a Skill is a Cowork feature still exclusive to Claude Cowork on Mac desktops with Pro, Max, and Team plans, but we’ll get into that later.
Claude automatically selects and uses skills depending on the context. You don’t have to tell it when to use a skill or which one to invoke, though you can do so in a few ways:
1. When creating a skill, you can include explicit wording in the skill description on how Claude can know when to invoke the skill ( Anthropic recommends writing in third person ). Example: “Use this skill whenever the user says ‘generate an image,’ ‘make an infographic,’ or ‘create an image.’”
2. Add the instructions to your prompt. Example: “Use your infographic skill to create a bar chart showing the monthly sales comparison.”
As a marketer, I’m often overwhelmed by the sheer number of features that Claude offers (and new ones get released seemingly every week!). So, here’s a quick demystifier on the difference between Claude skills, projects, instructions, and memory.
Which one you use depends on what problem you’re running into:
As Alex Banks puts it : “Skills are the tools in the workshop. Projects are the workshop itself.”
These four can also be combined: A single project can carry its own instructions and project-specific memory while you invoke skills inside it.
Claude plugins bundle skills, MCP connectors, commands, and agents into one package.
Adding a skill doesn’t “retrain” or “fine-tune” Claude, and it doesn’t change how the model thinks. A skill is simply a set of task-specific instructions Claude reads at the moment you need them, like handing a colleague an SOP and asking them to follow it.
Claude reads the skill using progressive disclosure : It brings a skill into the session piece by piece as needed, rather than all at once. Progressive disclosure works in three stages:
The benefit of this is that a skill can bundle large brand guidelines, datasets, or utilities without slowing down every conversation, because none of it loads until Claude needs it.
This article covers two ways to create a Claude Cowork skill:
If you already have a skill file, you can also upload it as a ZIP from Customize > Skills .
When I first learned about Claude Cowork skills, I had a hard time deciding what exactly I should turn into a skill. If you’re in the same boat, I recommend starting with any saved prompts or those you repeatedly type. Comb through your old chats and Claude projects and see what prompts or instructions you frequently use. Or if you have a prompt library in a spreadsheet or doc, mine that for ideas of what you can turn into a skill.
You can also spend one day observing what tasks you repeatedly carry out but have never documented. Capture these workflows by using Claude’s “Record a skill.”
Claude for Mac’s “Record a skill” feature is perfect for multi-step workflows you do all the time but have never formally documented. Anything where you can record a screenshare video while verbally walking through each step in under ten minutes is an ideal candidate. Some examples:
Below, I’ll walk you through the steps to use the “Record a skill” feature to make your first Claude Cowork skill. To demonstrate, I created a test skill for routing webinar leads for a fictional company using fake contacts.
1. In a Claude desktop app session, click + and select Record a skill from the dropdown menu.
2. You’ll get a pop-up. Click the Start recording button.
3. Start showing the workflow you want to turn into a skill, and be sure to narrate each step that you’re taking. Think of it like filming a Loom for a coworker — you need to give all the context so Claude knows why you did each thing. You’ll know Claude is recording when a coral-colored halo surrounds your screen, and an overlay appears at the bottom showing “Capturing” and a timer.
4. When you’re done showing the workflow, click the Done button.
5. Once you click Done, Claude will automatically open a new session with a prompt that says “I recorded a demonstration of a desktop workflow for you to learn from” and start building the skill. You do not have to do anything but wait for it to finish.
6. When Claude is finished and delivers the skill, click Content to expand the instructions and read the skill to ensure it’s what you want.
7. After reviewing the contents, if you’re happy with it, click the Save button. If you want to make changes, ask Claude to make updates to the skill within the chat. It will then deliver an updated skill, and you must click the Update button to save the changes.
8. After you save your new skill, check to make sure it appears in Customize > Skills . Now, it’s ready to use! Click + and Add folder to give Cowork access to the folder with the files it needs to read and modify for this task. I recommend testing the Claude Cowork skill on dummy data first to ensure it works properly before trying it on a real task.
I tested my new webinar-lead-routing skill on fake contacts, and it worked exactly as I’d described it in the recording.
Proving month-end marketing wins to leadership can be a challenge when you’ve got so many reports and dashboards to pull from. A performance-memo skill turns a folder of channel exports into a one-page summary in your preferred reporting format.
Example input: “September exports: Google Ads, LinkedIn Ads, GA4, webinar platform. Plan: 1,200 registrations, $85 cost per lead.”
When a prospect sends contracts back with redlines, it can take days for legal to review, which can stall the deal. A redline-triage skill sorts a prospect’s changes against your approved fallback positions before the file reaches legal — so the team doesn’t waste time reviewing cases already outlined by your playbook.
Example input: “Copperline Foods returned our MSA. Payment terms changed from Net 30 to Net 60, liability cap raised to 2x annual fees, new termination-for-convenience clause.”
Support teams sometimes first hear about a product change from a confused customer. A release-briefing skill converts engineering’s release notes into an internal briefing so agents are ready before launch.
Example input: “Release 4.12: CSV export moves from Settings to Reports. Exports over 50,000 rows now arrive by email.”
Use caution with Claude Cowork because it can read, write, and delete files from the folders you point it to (with your permission, of course). I think this Claude Academy lesson paints the picture best with this analogy:
“ Pointing Claude at Documents, Downloads, or Desktop is the equivalent of letting a new colleague rummage through every file you have. Make a folder for the work. Move (or copy) in what’s needed. Point Claude there.”
On top of the access you grant Claude through Cowork, skills downloaded from the internet can contain malicious code, so it’s important to know where the skill came from and review its content before installing.
This section covers the basics of how to keep your data safe while using Claude Cowork skills. For a deeper dive, I recommend reading Claude Support’s article on using Cowork safely .
Everything visible during a recording is evidence for the model. Claude’s safety regulations recommend :
A skill built on a real spreadsheet can carry names, account numbers, or internal URLs into a document you later share with others. So, build the skill on filler data. Test it on real data only after you review it.
Before you use, share, or deploy a skill to your team, check these items:
Skills are useful for detailing how to do a task, but they can’t on their own get up-to-date information about your business and customers. So if a workflow depends on a deal stage or sales call notes, you would have to manually enter that yourself — unless you have a connector.
This is what the HubSpot connector for Claude does. It’s an official MCP (Model Context Protocol) connector built by HubSpot that gives Claude read and write access to your CRM — directly from the Claude chat window.
The connector is a permission-based integration. You connect it once via OAuth; a Super Admin or user with HubSpot Marketplace permissions must authorize it in your HubSpot account first.
It also does not support delete operations. It also does not access HubSpot Sensitive Data properties. If your account has Sensitive Data enabled, it affects engagement data access as well — verify with your admin before building workflows on top of it.
Pro tip: Set the connector’s write tools to “Needs Approval” in Claude, as HubSpot recommends, so nothing changes until you confirm it.
Also worth knowing: according to HubSpot’s connector page , Anthropic does not use information shared through HubSpot to train its models, except when you choose to provide feedback or opt in.
1. Pre-call brief skill: Before a meeting, ask: “Pull everything we know about [Company] and give me a one-page brief.” The connector fetches the contact record, recent notes, open deals, and engagement history. The skill structures the output: background, open items, suggested talking points.
2. Post-call note and update skill: After a call, describe what happened in plain language. The skill formats a note in your standard structure. The connector logs it to the right deal or contact in HubSpot. No tab-switching required.
3. Pipeline review skill: “Which deals in Negotiation haven’t been touched in 10+ days?” The connector pulls the data; the skill formats it as a prioritized list with suggested next actions per deal.
4. Lead enrichment skill: When a new contact comes in, trigger a brief: company overview, LinkedIn context (if you’ve added a web search tool), recent news. Attach a suggested outreach opener. Log the research as a note.
These workflows live in the HubSpot connector for Claude — explore it here .
Yes, skills enabled in Cowork also work in Claude Code because they sync whenever you sign in with the same Claude account (as long as you have v2.1.273 or later). However, it’s a one-way sync — so skills you install in Claude Code do not sync with Claude Cowork or chat. Skills also work in Claude Chat. They’re a Claude-level feature, and the only Cowork-exclusive feature was Record a Skill, which still has some limitations since the September 2026 merger of Cowork and Chat.
Use fake test data instead of real customer data when recording your skill. Anthropic warns against displaying sensitive information while recording, because anything visible on your screen or spoken aloud during the session is captured. Test with real data only after you’ve reviewed the generated skill carefully, since it can carry visible information into a reusable document.
On Team and Enterprise plans, once an owner turns on sharing, open Customize > Skills , click the three-dot menu beside a skill you built, and choose Share . You can then add people by name or email. Recipients get a view-only copy that picks up your edits the next time they use it. Admins can control what’s published to the org directory, and recorded skills default to private until the creator shares them. Cowork keeps internal version history per skill, so you can roll back if an update breaks something. On Team plans, there’s a soft cap of 50 custom skills per workspace; Enterprise caps at 200.
Skills are invoked only as needed when the context calls for them in a conversation, whereas profile instructions apply globally across all chats at all times. Skills are a narrow set of instructions for a particular task, whereas projects are broader containers that can hold documents, project-specific instructions, project-specific memory, and conversations opened within that project. Memory stores facts about you that persist across conversations. These features complement each other: a project can house the context that a skill then acts on.
Install the HubSpot connector for Claude , which is available on any HubSpot plan (even free) alongside a paid Claude subscription . Open Claude’s Settings > Connectors , browse for HubSpot , click Connect , and pick permissions. Unless you’re a Super Admin or have App Marketplace Access, a Super Admin must approve the connector. Claude sees only what your HubSpot permissions allow, and it can create and update records, but it cannot delete them . Once connected, you can ask Claude about your CRM from any conversation.
The biggest mistake people make with Claude skills is trying to automate everything at once. They build ten skills before they’ve tested one, and end up with a junk drawer nobody uses.
A better approach: pick the one task your team does every week that follows the same steps every time. A report. A brief. A follow-up sequence. Build a skill for that, test it on messy inputs, and get it working reliably before you add another.
Once that first skill is running, connecting it to live data is what takes it from a time-saver to an actual workflow. That’s where the HubSpot connector for Claude comes in.
Skills handle the how. The connector supplies the what. Together, they’re the closest thing to a reliable AI teammate that doesn’t need to be briefed from scratch every Monday.
Ready to try it? Explore the HubSpot connector for Claude and connect your CRM context to the workflows you’re already building.
